claim: Adult male C57Bl/6 mice were conditioned to associate moving gratings of identical orientation, but presented at different locations in the visual field, with upcoming reward or absence of reward.
source: Adult male C57Bl/6 mice were conditioned to associate moving gratings of identical orientation, but presented at different locations in the visual field, with upcoming reward or absence of reward (Figure 1a,b,d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and references figures showing the setup and stimuli.

claim: Animals were exposed to the conditioning paradigm for 10 to 17 daily sessions of 40 to 60 trials each.
source: Animals were exposed to the conditioning paradigm for 10 to 17 daily sessions of 40 to 60 trials each (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of sessions and trials, with reference to a figure showing the timeline.

claim: From the first conditioning session onwards, putative licks and sniffs emerged aligned to stimulus onset, offset, reward arm movement onset, and reward delivery.
source: From the first conditioning session onwards, putative licks and sniffs emerged aligned to stimulus onset (−6 s), offset (−2 s), reward arm movement onset (−0.5 s) and reward delivery (0 s; Figure 1f, left panel and Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal patterns of behavioral responses with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Initially there were no differences in behavioral responses between rewarded trials and non-rewarded trials, up to the time of reward consumption.
source: Initially there were no differences in behavioral responses between rewarded trials and non-rewarded trials, up to the time of reward consumption (Wilcoxon Matched-Pairs Signed-Rank (WMPSR) test; Nasal movement: p=0.32; Oral movement: p=0.90, n = 10 mice; Figure 1f–g and Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant differences initially.

claim: From the second conditioning session onwards, a difference in anticipatory oral and nasal movements began to emerge between rewarded and non-rewarded trials in the period of reward-arm movement.
source: From the second conditioning session onwards, however, a difference in anticipatory oral and nasal movements began to emerge between rewarded and non-rewarded trials in the period of reward-arm movement, defined from −0.4 s to −0.16 s before (non-) reward time (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the emergence of behavioral differences with temporal specificity and figure references.

claim: On the last day, all but one mouse showed increased nasal and oral movements during the reward-anticipation period.
source: On the last day, all but one mouse showed increased nasal and oral movements during this reward-anticipation period (WMPSR test; Last day; Oral movements: p=0.004; Nasal movements: p=0.004, n = 10 mice; Figure 1g,h and Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing significant increases in anticipatory movements.

claim: The conditioning related increases in anticipatory nasal and oral movements during reward arm movement most likely reflect learned expectation of reward delivery.
source: Therefore, the conditioning related increases in anticipatory nasal and oral movements during reward arm movement most likely reflect learned expectation of reward delivery.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the behavioral data based on the temporal pattern of responses.

claim: Pupil location and pupil diameter were tracked in six animals over the entire course of the behavioral experiment.
source: Therefore, pupil location and pupil diameter were tracked in six animals over the entire course of the behavioral experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the eye-tracking methodology with reference to a figure.

claim: There was a slight but systematic bias of pupil orientation towards the location of a presented stimulus along the vertical axis.
source: This revealed a slight but systematic bias of pupil orientation towards the location of a presented stimulus along the vertical axis (Data combined across last 4 days, WMPSR test, Vertical: p=0.00091, Horizontal: p=0.39, n = 6 mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 3b–g).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant vertical bias in eye position.

claim: The amplitude of the shift in vertical eye position did not differ by more than 1.0 retinal degrees.
source: Nonetheless, the amplitude of the shift in vertical eye position did not differ by more than 1.0 retinal degrees (Online Materials and methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d).
evidence: The manuscript provides a quantitative measure of eye movement amplitude.

claim: V1 receptive fields in the mouse cover much larger regions (i.e. diameter ≧10 retinal degrees).
source: Given that V1 receptive fields in the mouse cover much larger regions (i.e. diameter ≧10 retinal degrees; Smith and Häusser, 2010; Bonin et al., 2011) and that the conditioned stimulus size was 30 retinal degrees (Azimuth and Elevation), this subtle variation in eye position did not strongly reduce the retinotopic specificity of the visual stimulus during conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to support the claim about receptive field sizes.

claim: The conditioned stimulus size was 30 retinal degrees (Azimuth and Elevation).
source: Given that V1 receptive fields in the mouse cover much larger regions (i.e. diameter ≧10 retinal degrees; Smith and Häusser, 2010; Bonin et al., 2011) and that the conditioned stimulus size was 30 retinal degrees (Azimuth and Elevation), this subtle variation in eye position did not strongly reduce the retinotopic specificity of the visual stimulus during conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific size of the visual stimulus used.

claim: The subtle variation in eye position did not strongly reduce the retinotopic specificity of the visual stimulus during conditioning.
source: Given that V1 receptive fields in the mouse cover much larger regions (i.e. diameter ≧10 retinal degrees; Smith and Häusser, 2010; Bonin et al., 2011) and that the conditioned stimulus size was 30 retinal degrees (Azimuth and Elevation), this subtle variation in eye position did not strongly reduce the retinotopic specificity of the visual stimulus during conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript provides a logical inference based on the comparison of eye movement amplitude, receptive field size, and stimulus size.

claim: During the reward delivery period, eye movements and pupil dilations were more pronounced.
source: During the reward delivery period, eye movements and pupil dilations were more pronounced.
evidence: The manuscript describes increased eye movements and pupil changes during reward delivery.

claim: The eye position showed a downward gaze-shift, potentially to the incoming reward spout.
source: The eye position showed a downward gaze-shift, potentially to the incoming reward spout (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the direction of eye movement with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Dilation of the pupil may have indicated arousal as a consequence of reward consumption.
source: Dilation of the pupil may have indicated arousal as a consequence of reward consumption (Data combined across last 4 days: WMPSR test, p=7.1⋅10−5, n = 6 mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 3i,j; Bradley et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical evidence for pupil dilation and cites a reference to support the interpretation.

claim: Head restrained mice make eye-movement responses and show pupillary reactions to behaviorally relevant stimuli, like rewards.
source: Thus, despite the lack of foveal vision, head restrained mice make eye-movement responses and show pupillary reactions to behaviorally relevant stimuli, like rewards.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the eye-tracking findings.

claim: Differences in eye movements and pupillary reactions between rewarded and non-rewarded trials were large during the reward delivery phase.
source: Differences in these behaviors between rewarded and non-rewarded trials were large during the reward delivery phase, while during stimulus presentation differences between the upper and lower visual field were negligible.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal pattern of differences in eye-related behaviors.

claim: During stimulus presentation differences in eye movements between the upper and lower visual field were negligible.
source: Differences in these behaviors between rewarded and non-rewarded trials were large during the reward delivery phase, while during stimulus presentation differences between the upper and lower visual field were negligible.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal pattern of differences in eye-related behaviors.

claim: Repeated transcranial imaging of intrinsic optical signals in area V1 of anesthetized mice was used to follow the cortical retinotopic organization throughout learning.
source: To follow the cortical retinotopic organization throughout learning, we used repeated transcranial imaging of intrinsic optical signals in area V1 of anesthetized mice.
evidence: The manuscript describes the imaging methodology used.

claim: The response amplitude to the non-rewarded, trained stimulus was decreased after conditioning when compared to before conditioning.
source: Using this method, we observed that the response amplitude to the non-rewarded, trained stimulus was decreased after conditioning when compared to before conditioning (amplitude of non-rewarded minus orthogonal, across time points: Kruskal-Wallis, normalized per mouse, H(2, 24)=13.15, p=0.0014, post hoc WMPSR test, Before vs. After, p=0.0039; n = 9 mice; Figure 2d,g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant decrease in response amplitude.

claim: The response amplitude to the rewarded conditioned stimulus was not significantly reduced at the time point after conditioning.
source: The response amplitude to the rewarded conditioned stimulus was not significantly reduced at the time point after conditioning (amplitude of rewarded minus orthogonal, mouse-normalized, across time points: Kruskal-Wallis, normalized per mouse, H(2, 24)=6.39, p=0.041, post hoc WMPSR test, Before vs. After, p=0.57, n = 9 mice).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant reduction in response amplitude for the rewarded stimulus.

claim: After conditioning, the IOS ΔOverlap was significantly reduced in the cortical region that responded to the rewarded stimulus.
source: After conditioning (i.e., on day 11–18), the IOS ΔOverlap was significantly reduced in the cortical region that responded to the rewarded stimulus (Kruskal-Wallis test, normalized per mouse, H(2,24) = 10.00, p=0.0067, post hoc WMPSR test, Before vs. After, p=0.020, n = 9 mice; Figure 2f,h).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant reduction in overlap.

claim: In the region responding to the non-rewarded stimulus, the IOS ΔOverlap was not significantly reduced as a function of training.
source: In the region responding to the non-rewarded stimulus, the IOS ΔOverlap was not significantly reduced as a function of training (Kruskal-Wallis test, normalized per mouse, H(2,24) = 0.98, p=0.61, n = 9 mice; Figure 2f,h).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant reduction in overlap for the non-rewarded region.

claim: After training, the IOS ΔOverlap in the cortical region representing the rewarded stimulus was significantly reduced compared to the region mostly responsive to the non-rewarded stimulus.
source: After training, the IOS ΔOverlap in the cortical region representing the rewarded stimulus was significantly reduced compared to the region mostly responsive to the non-rewarded stimulus (WSRMP test, p=0.039, n = 9 mice; Figure 2f,h).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant difference between regions.

claim: Spatial selectivity index showed a similar effect of sharpened spatial selectivity for the rewarded condition and location.
source: Because the measure of overlap is sensitive to the absolute response amplitude, we also quantified the mesoscopic segregation of intrinsic cortical responses using a ratiometric index, the spatial selectivity index. This showed a similar effect of sharpened spatial selectivity for the rewarded condition and location (Kruskal-Wallis test, mouse-normalized, H(2,24) = 6.16, p=0.046, WMPSR test, rewarded vs. non-rewarded, p=0.039, n = 9 mice; Figure 2i).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing sharpened spatial selectivity.

claim: The magnitude of IOS-ΔOverlap, selectivity for stimulus location, and response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus correlated strongly within individual mice.
source: The magnitude of these above-mentioned effects ('IOS-ΔOverlap', 'selectivity for stimulus location' and 'response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus') correlated strongly within individual mice (IOS-ΔOverlap × Selectivity: r = −0.94, p=0.0002, n = 9 mice; Amplitude × Selectivity: r = 0.81, p=0.008, n = 9 mice; Amplitude × ΔOverlap: r = −0.65, p=0.058, n = 9 mice), which suggests that they resulted from closely related mechanisms that operated on the rewarded as well as the non-rewarded side of the stimulus representation.
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics and interprets them as evidence for related mechanisms.

claim: The distance between the peaks in the intrinsic response profiles did not significantly increase despite a trend.
source: Finally, to test whether the representation of the rewarded and non-rewarded trained stimuli drifted apart in cortical space, we quantified the distance between the peaks in the intrinsic response profiles. Despite a trend, this measure of spatial distance between trained stimulus representations did not significantly increase (Kruskal-Wallis test, normalized per mouse, H(2,24) = 0.57, p=0.75, n = 9 mice; Figure 2j).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant increase in distance.

claim: Classical conditioning, using rewarded and non-rewarded stimuli that occupy neighboring regions of visual space, selectively reshaped the retinotopic organization for the trained stimuli compared to control stimuli, while the overall representations of the trained stimuli did not significantly drift apart.
source: Hence, classical conditioning, using rewarded and non-rewarded stimuli that occupy neighboring regions of visual space, selectively reshaped the retinotopic organization for the trained stimuli compared to control stimuli, while the overall representations of the trained stimuli did not significantly drift apart.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings from the intrinsic imaging experiments.

claim: OGB1-calcium imaging was performed after the final conditioning session.
source: To understand how formation of a visuospatial stimulus-reward association affects neuronal response properties within the retinotopic representation, we performed OGB1-calcium imaging (Stosiek et al., 2003) after the final conditioning session (Figure 3a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the timing and methodology of calcium imaging with a citation.

claim: Recordings were made in multiple V1-subregions per animal, positioned along the rewarded/non-rewarded axis within V1.
source: Recordings were made in multiple V1-subregions per animal, positioned along the rewarded/non-rewarded axis within V1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial distribution of recording locations.

claim: Every field-of-view was assigned to a cortical location group based on the population response amplitude to visual stimulation in each of the retinotopic locations using moving gratings of non-trained orientations.
source: Every field-of-view was assigned to a cortical location group; Full non-rewarded, Border non-rewarded, Border rewarded and Full rewarded, based on the population response amplitude to visual stimulation in each of the retinotopic locations using moving gratings of non-trained orientations (Online Materials and methods; Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification method for recording locations.

claim: The Ca2+ ΔOverlap was significantly lower for imaging fields in the full rewarded region and at the rewarded/non-rewarded location border, compared to field-of-views that were located fully in the non-rewarded stimulus region.
source: The Ca2+ ΔOverlap was significantly lower for imaging fields in the full rewarded region and at the rewarded/non-rewarded location border, compared to field-of-views that were located fully in the non-rewarded stimulus region (Kruskal-Wallis test, H(3,45) = 11.6, p=0.0088, n = 49 imaging fields; Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing significant differences in overlap across regions.

claim: The pattern of overlap in location selective responses based on calcium imaging data resembled the results obtained using intrinsic signal imaging.
source: The pattern of overlap in location selective responses based on calcium imaging data resembled the results obtained using intrinsic signal imaging (Gray line in Figure 3c indicates IOS ΔOverlap as in Figure 2d), showing the strongest reduction in Overlap (as compared to control) in the Border rewarded and Border non-rewarded regions.
evidence: The manuscript compares results from two imaging methods with reference to figures.

claim: Selectivity for retinotopic location, calculated using calcium imaging data, was larger in the Full rewarded and Border rewarded regions, as compared to the Full non-rewarded region.
source: Also selectivity for retinotopic location, now calculated using calcium imaging data, was larger in the Full rewarded and Border rewarded regions, as compared to the Full non-rewarded region (Kruskal-Wallis test, H(3,45) = 19.3, p=0.0024, n = 49 imaging fields).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing significant differences in selectivity across regions.

claim: The measured ΔOverlap in the rewarded stimulus location correlated strongly and significantly across methods (IOS vs. Ca2+).
source: The measured ΔOverlap in the rewarded stimulus location correlated strongly and significantly across methods (IOS vs. Ca2+, r = 0.81, p=0.016, n = 8 mice) and a weaker, but similarly positive correlation was found for retinotopic location selectivity (r = 0.69, p=0.058, n = 8 mice).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics comparing results from two imaging methods.

claim: The fraction of responsive cells per stimulus orientation was significantly reduced in the Full rewarded location.
source: Interestingly, the fraction of responsive cells per stimulus orientation was significantly reduced in the Full rewarded location and did not differ significantly between the Border rewarded and Border non-rewarded locations (2-way Anova, interaction effect of Location bin versus Preferred orientation, F(3,90) = 3.99, p=0.010; n = 49 recordings; Post hoc, Trained versus Orthogonal orientation for full-rewarded location: p<0.05; Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant reduction in responsive cells.

claim: The population response amplitude to rewarded stimuli increased more steeply from Border non-rewarded locations to Border rewarded locations compared to the increase of the population response to non-rewarded stimuli from Border rewarded to Border non-rewarded locations.
source: Instead, we observed that the population response amplitude to rewarded stimuli increased more steeply from Border non-rewarded locations to Border rewarded locations compared to the increase of the population response to non-rewarded stimuli from Border rewarded to Border non-rewarded locations (2-way Anova, interaction effect of location vs. population response difference, Trained stimuli: F(3,85) = 3.59, p=0.017, Untrained stimuli: F(3,85) = 1.48, p=0.23; n = 49 recordings; Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant interaction effect for trained stimuli.

claim: The reduction in response amplitude (trained orientation minus orthogonal control), as obtained using calcium imaging, covaried with the reduction in response amplitude that was observed in the intrinsic imaging data.
source: Nonetheless, the reduction in response amplitude (trained orientation minus orthogonal control), as obtained using calcium imaging, did covary with the reduction in response amplitude that was observed in the intrinsic imaging data (IOS vs. Ca2+, r = 0.92, p=0.028, n = 5 mice for which we had both intrinsic imaging data and calcium imaging recordings from the non-rewarded location).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics comparing results from two imaging methods.

claim: The observed mesoscopic disambiguation of the representation of the rewarded and non-rewarded stimulus is expressed at the single neuron level.
source: These results suggest that the observed mesoscopic disambiguation of the representation of the rewarded and non-rewarded stimulus (as observed using intrinsic imaging) is expressed at the single neuron level (as observed using calcium imaging) and is potentially mediated by a spatially restricted change in response patterns of a select population of neurons, rather than an overall expansion of the cortical map for rewarded or non-rewarded stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the combined imaging results.

claim: The mesoscopic disambiguation is potentially mediated by a spatially restricted change in response patterns of a select population of neurons, rather than an overall expansion of the cortical map for rewarded or non-rewarded stimuli.
source: These results suggest that the observed mesoscopic disambiguation of the representation of the rewarded and non-rewarded stimulus (as observed using intrinsic imaging) is expressed at the single neuron level (as observed using calcium imaging) and is potentially mediated by a spatially restricted change in response patterns of a select population of neurons, rather than an overall expansion of the cortical map for rewarded or non-rewarded stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the combined imaging results.

claim: The percentage of cells that preferred the rewarded and non-rewarded stimulus location was similar, although not identical.
source: On average, the percentage of cells that preferred the rewarded and non-rewarded stimulus location was similar, although not identical (total: 32.2%, see Table 1 for fraction per mouse; rewarded: 17.8%, non-rewarded: 14.5%; WMPSR-test, p=0.58, n = 11 mice; Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript provides percentages and statistical test results.

claim: The relative fractions of cells preferring trained and other orientations differed significantly between groups that were tuned to rewarded and non-rewarded locations.
source: However, the relative fractions of cells preferring trained and other orientations differed significantly between groups that were tuned to rewarded and non-rewarded locations (these fractions were normalized to the overall fraction of responsive neurons per mouse, across all preferred orientations and locations and adjusted for relative bin width so that the expected fraction given a flat distribution of preferred orientations was 1.0; Figure 4b,c).
evidence: The manuscript describes a significant difference with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: For cells tuned to the rewarded location there was a relatively smaller fraction of cells preferring the trained orientation, compared to the set of cells that responded to the non-rewarded orientation.
source: Specifically, for cells tuned to the rewarded location there was a relatively smaller fraction of cells preferring the trained orientation, compared to the set of cells that responded to the non-rewarded (i.e. orthogonal) orientation (Kruskal-Wallis test, 'Rewarded−Non-rewarded' vs. 'ΔOri. from trained', H(4,50) = 9.76, p=0.045; post hoc WMPSR-test, '0°–10°' vs. '50°–70°', p=0.042, n = 11 mice; Figure 4d).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing a significant difference in cell fractions.

claim: Although fewer neurons were significantly responsive to the conditioned stimulus orientation, the individual neurons that responded to the rewarded stimulus did so more strongly.
source: Although the fraction of cells tuned to the conditioned orientation at the rewarded stimulus location was reduced, their response amplitude to the trained orientation was increased compared to cells responding to the non-rewarded location (Kruskal-Wallis test, 'Rewarded−Non-rewarded' vs. 'ΔOri. from trained', H(4,48) = 11.6, p=0.020; n = 11 mice; Figure 4e).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing increased response amplitude despite reduced cell fraction.

claim: Neurons with tuning curves that flanked the preferred orientation had broader tuning curves.
source: Moreover, neurons with tuning curves that flanked the preferred orientation (ΔOri. from trained between 10° and 30°) had broader tuning curves (Kruskal-Wallis test, 'ΔOri. from trained', H(4,48) = 14.1, p=0.0068; Post hoc WMPSR test, '0°–10°' vs. '10°–30°', p=0.0039; n = 11 mice; Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing broader tuning curves for flanking neurons.

claim: Neurons with preferred orientations that slightly differ from the trained orientation increased their response to the trained orientation, rendering their orientation tuning curves broader.
source: The latter effect indicates that neurons with preferred orientations that slightly differ from the trained orientation increased their response to the trained orientation (regardless of the reward-location association), rendering their orientation tuning curves broader (Goltstein et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the tuning curve data with a citation to previous work.

claim: The orientation selectivity index did not significantly differ between rewarded and non-rewarded tuned neurons, or as function of angle between preferred orientation and the trained orientation.
source: The orientation selectivity index did not significantly differ between rewarded and non-rewarded tuned neurons, or as function of angle between preferred orientation and the trained orientation (Kruskal-Wallis test, p>0.16; n = 11 mice).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant differences.

claim: The population response to trained stimuli in the rewarded location did not show a significantly lower sparseness compared to the population response to visual stimulation in the non-rewarded location.
source: In order to test whether the differences described above reflected an overall sparser population response to rewarded conditioned stimuli, we quantified population sparseness (ap, lower values indicate a sparser population response; Rolls and Treves, 2011) for the tuning curve response of all neurons. The population response to trained stimuli in the rewarded location did not show a significantly lower sparseness compared to the population response to visual stimulation in the non-rewarded location (Kruskal-Wallis test, 'ΔOri. from trained', H(4,50) = 0.23, p=0.99; n = 11 mice; Figure 4g).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant difference in sparseness.

claim: After training, the cortical map for trained stimulus location and orientation became more selective for retinotopic position.
source: Thus far our data obtained using intrinsic signal imaging as well as calcium imaging indicate that, after training, the cortical map for trained stimulus location and orientation became more selective for retinotopic position.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from both imaging methods.

claim: Populations of simultaneously recorded single neurons would show an improved ability to discriminate the location of trained stimuli as compared to the (same) locations of untrained control stimuli.
source: We therefore hypothesized that populations of simultaneously recorded single neurons would show an improved ability to discriminate the location of trained stimuli as compared to the (same) locations of untrained control stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript states a hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: In the population of significantly tuned Border neurons, decoding of stimulus location was significantly better for the trained orientation as compared to the orthogonal orientation.
source: First, we decoded calcium responses recorded in field-of-views located around the rewarded/non-rewarded border on the cortical surface (see Figures 3b and 5a, inset left). In this population of significantly tuned Border neurons, decoding of stimulus location was significantly better for the trained orientation as compared to the orthogonal orientation (WMPSR test, difference between 'trained' and 'orthogonal orientation' averaged across all sample sizes per mouse, p=0.0078; n = 9 mice; Figure 5a, left panel).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing better decoding for trained stimuli.

claim: Decoding of activity patterns from cells recorded in regions further away from the border did not differ between trained and untrained orientations.
source: Decoding of activity patterns from cells recorded in regions further away from the border (see Figure 5a, right panel) did not differ between trained and untrained orientations (WMPSR test, difference between 'trained' and 'orthogonal orientation' averaged across all sample sizes per mouse, p=0.46; n = 11 mice; Figure 5a, right panel).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no difference in decoding for non-border regions.

claim: The magnitude of the difference in decoding performance between trained and other orientations correlated significantly with the magnitude of the difference in anticipatory nasal and oral movements in the behavioral paradigm.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of the difference in decoding performance between trained and other (45° and 90°) orientations correlated significantly with the magnitude of the difference in anticipatory nasal and oral movements in the behavioral paradigm (Nasal movements: r = 0.83, p=0.041; Oral movements: r = 0.96, p=0.003; n = 6 mice; Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics linking neural decoding to behavior.

claim: Decoding performance did not correlate significantly with the total number of conditioning trials that the mice were exposed to.
source: Decoding performance did not correlate significantly with the total number of conditioning trials that the mice were exposed to (Total number of trials: r = −0.18, p=0.73; n = 6 mice).
evidence: The manuscript provides correlation statistics showing no relationship between decoding and trial number.

claim: There were no significant differences in average signal correlations and noise correlations between the trained and control orientations.
source: Signal and noise correlations were calculated on tuning curves of all simultaneously recorded pairs of cells that were either responsive to the rewarded or non-rewarded location and grouped according to the similarity of their preferred orientations relative to the trained orientation, and whether they were located in the Full or Border stimulus region. However, there were no significant differences in average signal correlations and noise correlations between the trained and control orientations (Bootstrap confidence intervals, p>0.05; Figure 6a).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing no significant differences in correlations.

claim: In the border imaging regions, high signal correlation pairs that were tuned to the trained orientations exhibited significantly lower noise correlations compared to pairs preferring other orientations.
source: In the border imaging regions, high signal correlation pairs that were tuned to the trained orientations exhibited significantly lower noise correlations compared to pairs preferring other orientations (Bootstrap confidence intervals, p<0.01; nborder = 20 imaging fields of view; Figure 6b, right panel, solid lines).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing lower noise correlations for high signal correlation pairs.

claim: In the Full imaging regions, low signal correlation pairs had stronger noise correlations when they were tuned to the trained orientations as compared to the control orientations.
source: In addition, in the Full imaging regions, we observed that low signal correlation pairs had stronger noise correlations when they were tuned to the trained orientations as compared to the control orientations (Bootstrap confidence intervals, p<0.05; nfull = 24 imaging fields of view; Figure 6b, left panel, dotted lines).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results showing stronger noise correlations for low signal correlation pairs.

claim: The effect of classical conditioning on noise correlations depends on the signal correlation of the pair of neurons, which can have the overall effect of enhancing the discriminability of trained stimuli in the population.
source: Thus, the effect of classical conditioning on noise correlations depends on the signal correlation of the pair of neurons, which can have the overall effect of enhancing the discriminability of trained stimuli in the population.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: Associative learning (by coupling a visual stimulus to reward) affects orientation-specific coding of single neurons in a retinotopically restricted fashion but fails to lead to an overall expansion of the cortical region representing the trained visual space.
source: Our results indicate how associative learning (by coupling a visual stimulus to reward) affects orientation-specific coding of single neurons in a retinotopically restricted fashion but fails to lead to an overall expansion of the cortical region representing the trained visual space, thus leaving the retinotopic map intact.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Learning-induced changes in single neurons emerge in concert with enhanced stimulus representations at the population level increasing location discriminability within the V1 cortical map.
source: These data demonstrate that learning-induced changes in single neurons emerge in concert with enhanced stimulus representations at the population level increasing location discriminability within the V1 cortical map.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The central finding in this study is improved coding for stimulus location by a population of neurons that preferred the trained orientation and was located within the cortical retinotopic region where the trained stimuli bordered.
source: The central finding in this study is improved coding for stimulus location by a population of neurons that preferred the trained orientation and was located within the cortical retinotopic region where the trained stimuli bordered.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the central finding.

claim: This enhanced selectivity for retinotopic location was observed using both a mesoscale (intrinsic imaging) and a microscale (calcium imaging) method.
source: This enhanced selectivity for retinotopic location was observed using both a mesoscale (intrinsic imaging) and a microscale (calcium imaging) method.
evidence: The manuscript states that both imaging methods showed the same effect.

claim: The data acquired using intrinsic imaging suggested that this effect was mediated by a reduction in response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus.
source: The data acquired using intrinsic imaging suggested that this effect was mediated by a reduction in response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus (Figure 2d,g).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the intrinsic imaging data with figure references.

claim: While visibly present, this reduction was less pronounced when observed at the single cell resolution using calcium imaging.
source: While visibly present, this reduction was less pronounced when observed at the single cell resolution using calcium imaging (Figure 3e).
evidence: The manuscript compares the magnitude of effects between imaging methods.

claim: The difference in results may be inherent to the difference in methods, with intrinsic signal imaging picking up a widespread mixed, metabolic signal across cortical neurons and layers, and with calcium imaging focusing on somatic spiking activity in layer 2/3 neurons selectively.
source: The difference in results may be inherent to the difference in methods, with intrinsic signal imaging picking up a widespread mixed, metabolic signal across cortical neurons (including dendrites, axons and synapses) and layers, and with calcium imaging focusing on somatic spiking activity in layer 2/3 neurons selectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative explanation for differences between methods based on their properties.

claim: The magnitude of reduction in trained stimulus-representation Overlap, as measured with each method, was correlated across mice, suggesting that the effects are related.
source: That the magnitude of reduction in trained stimulus-representation Overlap, as measured with each method (Figure 2f and Figure 3c), was correlated across mice suggests that the effects are related.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the correlation between methods.

claim: What was observed at the mesoscale as an overall change in response amplitude, may in part reflect a subtler change in stimulus selectivity or jointly orchestrated activity patterns at the single neuron, somatic level within cortical layer 2/3.
source: What was observed at the mesoscale as an overall change in response amplitude, may in part reflect a subtler change in stimulus selectivity or jointly orchestrated activity patterns at the single neuron, somatic level within cortical layer 2/3.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation of how mesoscale and microscale findings relate.

claim: The results obtained with calcium imaging were observed in comparison to untrained control orientations or control regions, and not compared to a hypothetical time point before learning.
source: It is of note that the results obtained with calcium imaging, such as differences in fraction and amplitude of responsive neurons and changes in population decoding for retinotopic location, were observed in comparison to untrained control orientations or control regions, and not compared to a hypothetical time point before learning.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation in the experimental design.

claim: It cannot be fully excluded that these effects were mediated, in part, by changes of the opposite sign in neurons that were tuned to untrained control orientations.
source: Therefore, it cannot be fully excluded that these effects were mediated, in part, by changes of the opposite sign in neurons that were tuned to untrained control orientations.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges an alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: Some effects of conditioning were quite selective for the trained orientation as compared to different untrained control orientations.
source: However, some effects of conditioning were quite selective for the trained orientation as compared to different untrained control (i.e. oblique and orthogonal) orientations (see e.g. Figures 4e and 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides evidence against the alternative interpretation by showing selectivity for trained stimuli.

claim: The trained orientation stood out from the way the broader population of untrained stimuli was processed.
source: While this does not fully confirm that learning effects were only present in neurons tuned to the trained orientation, it indicates that, at least, the trained orientation stood out from the way the broader population of untrained stimuli was processed.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the selectivity findings.

claim: Cortical representations have been known to exhibit plasticity.
source: Cortical representations, as also found in the auditory cortical tonotopic map or the somatosensory homunculus, have been known to exhibit plasticity (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Bao et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to support the claim about cortical plasticity.

claim: An example of map plasticity like observed here has not been found before in visual cortex.
source: An example of map plasticity like observed here, however, has not been found before in visual cortex, where shifts in retinotopic organization were, until now, described as a consequence of selectively depriving cortical input only (Heinen and Skavenski, 1991; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Keck et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty by contrasting with previous studies cited.

claim: The kind of refinement of the retinotopic map shown in these experiments is somewhat comparable to emerging discontinuities in the cortical digit representation after separation of webbed fingers or fading discontinuities in the somatosensory map after surgical syndactyly.
source: The kind of refinement of the retinotopic map as shown in our experiments—a sharper retinotopic gradient (Figure 3e) in calcium response patterns coupled to a reduced overlap in intrinsic optical responses (Figure 2e,f,h) and better location-decoding performance (Figure 5a)—is somewhat comparable to emerging discontinuities in the cortical digit representation after separation of webbed fingers (Mogilner et al., 1993) or fading discontinuities in the somatosensory map after surgical syndactyly (Allard et al., 1991).
evidence: The manuscript draws an analogy to previous studies with citations.

claim: Map-plasticity in previous studies emerged by self-organizing plasticity, while in this study, appetitive conditioning directed the alterations in the retinotopic map.
source: However, map-plasticity in these studies emerged by self-organizing plasticity, while in our study, appetitive conditioning directed the alterations in the retinotopic map.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the mechanism in this study with previous studies.

claim: Under naturalistic conditions stimulus-reward learning can direct functional changes in cortical maps, expressed in the way the cells in these maps encode sensory information.
source: Not only is the treatment (learning paradigm) more subtle than the interventions in the studies mentioned above, but the observed map-plasticity underscores that also under naturalistic conditions stimulus-reward learning can direct functional changes in cortical maps, expressed in the way the cells in these maps encode sensory information.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the findings in a broader context.

claim: Training to discriminate small differences in stimulus parameters can result in sharpening of tuning curves in the primary visual cortex.
source: The changes in neuronal tuning observed in our study can also be considered in the context of perceptual learning. Training to discriminate small differences in stimulus parameters can result in sharpening of tuning curves in the primary visual cortex (Schoups et al., 2001), an effect that has been suggested to help disambiguate fine differences in stimulus orientation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to provide context for the findings.

claim: The presently reported learning-induced reduction in overlap of the population response to trained stimuli resembles a mechanism of tuning curve sharpening, but now pertains to the cortical mapping of visual space.
source: The presently reported learning-induced reduction in overlap of the population response to trained stimuli resembles such a mechanism of tuning curve sharpening, but now pertains to the cortical mapping of visual space.
evidence: The manuscript draws an analogy between the current findings and previous work on tuning curve sharpening.

claim: A correlation was observed between the amount of anticipatory behavior and changes in neuronal population coding.
source: While our study did not directly compare the conditioned group with a sham-trained (randomly rewarded) group, we did observe a correlation between the amount of anticipatory behavior and changes in neuronal population coding (Figure 5), but no correlation to the number of trials.
evidence: The manuscript describes a correlation between behavior and neural changes.

claim: The observed effects are not merely the result of stimulus exposure but are associated with behavioral learning in the conditioning paradigm.
source: This argues that the observed effects are not merely the result of stimulus exposure but are associated with behavioral learning in the conditioning paradigm.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: Neuronal learning mechanisms underlying classic forms of map plasticity are generally thought to be Hebbian in nature.
source: Neuronal learning mechanisms underlying classic forms of map plasticity are generally thought to be Hebbian in nature (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998), functioning through rapid induction of LTP and LTD for spared and deprived inputs respectively or via competition between inputs (Feldman and Brecht, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to describe established mechanisms of plasticity.

claim: Local secretion of neurotransmitters like acetylcholine and noradrenaline plays a role in map plasticity.
source: Additionally, local secretion of neurotransmitters like acetylcholine and noradrenaline plays a role (Bear and Singer, 1986).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to describe neuromodulatory mechanisms.

claim: In auditory cortex, large shifts in tonotopic representations have been observed after pairing a tone with basal forebrain stimulation.
source: In auditory cortex for instance, large shifts in tonotopic representations have been observed after pairing a tone with basal forebrain stimulation (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to provide examples of neuromodulation-induced plasticity.

claim: In the current study, a large-scale expansion of the conditioned stimulus representation was not observed, but rather an increase in selectivity of the cortical map.
source: In the current study, we did not observe such a large-scale expansion of the conditioned stimulus representation, but rather an increase in selectivity of the cortical map.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the current findings with previous studies.

claim: Cholinergic neuromodulation can act to improve neuronal selectivity and perception in a rapid and task specific way.
source: Recent work in the primary visual cortex of the mouse has established that cholinergic neuromodulation can act to improve neuronal selectivity and perception in a rapid and task specific way (Pinto et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to describe a potential mechanism.

claim: During an appetitive conditioning paradigm, cholinergic input from basal forebrain to V1 induced strong local activity patterns leading up to the time of reward delivery, which may drive stimulus-selective plasticity.
source: Moreover, during an appetitive conditioning paradigm, cholinergic input from basal forebrain to V1 induced strong local activity patterns leading up to the time of reward delivery (Liu et al., 2015), which may drive stimulus-selective plasticity (Chubykin et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to describe a potential mechanism.

claim: The plasticity in V1's retinotopic map induced using appetitive conditioning may have been mediated by local release of acetylcholine.
source: The plasticity in V1's retinotopic map, which we induced here using appetitive conditioning, may therefore have been mediated by local release of acetylcholine.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation based on previous studies.

claim: The strengthening of feedback connections from higher visual or other cortices could provide an alternative or additional mechanism by which learning leads to changes in cortical maps.
source: However, the strengthening of feedback connections from higher visual or other cortices (Pennartz, 1997; Makino and Komiyama, 2015) could provide an alternative or additional mechanism by which learning leads to changes in cortical maps.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to describe an alternative mechanism.

claim: The observed reduction in response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus could indicate a role for an LTD type mechanism reducing excitatory drive of non-rewarded stimulus representation.
source: In addition, the observed reduction in response amplitude to the non-rewarded trained stimulus could indicate a role for an LTD type mechanism reducing excitatory drive of non-rewarded stimulus representation (Nabavi et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to describe a potential mechanism.

claim: The reduction in response amplitude could reflect strengthening of long-range lateral connections or feed-back from higher visual areas onto inhibitory neurons to increase local inhibitory drive of the non-rewarded stimulus representation.
source: Alternatively, it could reflect strengthening of long-range lateral connections from for example the rewarded retinotopic location, or feed-back from higher visual areas, onto inhibitory neurons in the non-rewarded retinotopic location to increase local inhibitory drive of the non-rewarded stimulus representation (Makino and Komiyama, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to describe an alternative mechanism.

claim: The conditioning-related improvement in retinotopic selectivity was observed under anesthesia, which makes it likely that these results depend to some degree on changes in feedforward or local recurrent synaptic connectivity.
source: While neuromodulation and long-range connectivity are strong candidates to mediate learning in our behavioral paradigm, the conditioning-related improvement in retinotopic selectivity was observed under anesthesia, which makes it likely that these results depend to some degree on changes in feedforward or local recurrent synaptic connectivity.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on the experimental conditions.

claim: Cells may increase their local connectivity with neurons that are tuned to the same retinotopic location, thereby strengthening their spatial selectivity but reducing precise selectivity for stimulus orientation.
source: We hypothesize that these cells increase their local connectivity with neurons that are tuned to the same retinotopic location, thereby strengthening their spatial selectivity (see Figures 2f,h and 3c–e) but reducing precise selectivity for stimulus orientation (see Figure 4f).
evidence: The manuscript provides a hypothesis based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Several theoretical studies have shown that reduction of noise correlations between cells exhibiting high signal correlations can improve population coding.
source: Several theoretical studies have shown that reduction of noise correlations between cells exhibiting high signal correlations can improve population coding (Zohary et al., 1994; Oram et al., 1998; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Averbeck et al., 2006; but see Montijn et al., 2016), but experimental evidence in support of these mechanisms being employed during learning is only sparsely available (Jeanne et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple theoretical and experimental studies to provide context.

claim: A decrease of noise correlations within high signal correlation pairs was strongest at the V1 location where the trained stimuli bordered.
source: Here, we show a decrease of noise correlations within high signal correlation pairs that was strongest at the V1 location where the trained stimuli bordered (Figure 6b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial pattern of correlation changes with figure reference.

claim: The findings provide support for the theoretical notion of how interactions between signal- and noise correlations can facilitate coding of stimulus information.
source: This provides support for the theoretical notion of how interactions between signal- and noise correlations can facilitate coding of stimulus information, and also shows that these effects can arise in the primary visual cortex as a result of associative learning.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the correlation findings in relation to theory.

claim: Groups of cells exhibiting low (negative) signal correlations may improve population coding by increasing noise correlations, even without transmitting information in the structure of the noise correlation itself.
source: In addition, groups of cells exhibiting low (negative) signal correlations may improve population coding by increasing noise correlations, even without transmitting information in the structure of the noise correlation itself (Oram et al., 1998; Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical studies to provide context for the findings.

claim: In imaging regions further away from the border of the trained stimuli, stronger noise correlations were observed in groups of trained orientation tuned cells with relatively low signal correlations.
source: Additionally, in imaging regions further away from the border of the trained stimuli, we observed stronger noise correlations in groups of trained orientation tuned cells with relatively low signal correlations.
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial pattern of correlation changes.

claim: This effect depends on how heterogeneously a population of neurons is tuned to the behaviorally relevant stimulus and therefore only manifested in the Full imaging regions.
source: Possibly this effect depends on how heterogeneously a population of neurons is tuned to the behaviorally relevant stimulus and therefore only manifested in the Full imaging regions where the majority neurons might have been synchronously driven by a single (rewarded or non-rewarded) stimulus.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation of the spatial pattern.

claim: Stimulus-reward pairing can enhance feature detection in primary visual cortex with or without stimulus awareness.
source: With or without stimulus awareness, stimulus-reward pairing can enhance feature detection in primary visual cortex (Shuler and Bear, 2006; Seitz et al., 2009; Frankó et al., 2010; Goltstein et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies to provide context.

claim: Visual conditioning resulted in a reduced fraction of neurons being tuned to the trained orientation in the rewarded location.
source: While we observed that visual conditioning resulted in a reduced fraction of neurons being tuned to the trained orientation in the rewarded location (Figures 3d and 4d), those neurons that remained to prefer the conditioned or similar orientations responded with larger ΔF/F amplitudes to the reward associated stimulus (Figure 4e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the changes in neuronal responses with figure references.

claim: Population coding for the conditioned orientation in the rewarded location contained fewer neurons compared to their untrained orientation tuned counterparts, while maintaining the average population response amplitude.
source: This indicates that population coding for the conditioned orientation in the rewarded location, contained fewer neurons compared to their untrained orientation tuned counterparts, while maintaining the average population response amplitude, thus potentially rendering their response more efficient by representing the same information using fewer cells (see also Gdalyahu et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the neuronal response changes with a citation.

claim: This study highlights a selective role for reward-dependent learning in refining the primary cortical retinotopic map.
source: In summary, this study highlights a selective role for reward-dependent learning in refining the primary cortical retinotopic map.
evidence: The manuscript provides a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Coordinated changes in neuronal tuning and inter-neuronal correlations can result in a more optimal population code for trained stimuli and improve the local representation of visual space while leaving the overall retinotopic map intact.
source: It demonstrates how coordinated changes in neuronal tuning and inter-neuronal correlations can result in a more optimal population code for trained stimuli and improve the local representation of visual space while leaving the overall retinotopic map intact.
